hints: Look closely at the chromosomes in cells 1, 2, 3 and 4. Which ones still have whole chromosomes together, and which ones already show sister chromatids pulled apart to opposite ends?
The drug only stops the spindle pulling sister chromatids apart. Think about which mitotic stages happen before that pulling, and which stages depend on that pulling having happened.
walkthrough:
**Identify the stages in the photos**

Look at what the chromosomes are doing. Cell 1 shows long, tangled condensing chromosomes, this is prophase. Cell 2 shows thick chromosomes arranged in the middle of the cell, this is metaphase.

Cell 3 shows two separate groups of chromatids moving to opposite poles, this is anaphase. Cell 4 shows two new nuclei forming, this is telophase with cytokinesis.

**Work out what the drug blocks**

The drug binds to the spindle and prevents sister chromatids being separated and moved to opposite poles. That pulling movement is the key event of anaphase. Without it, nothing after that point can happen normally.

**Decide which stages can still occur**

A cell entering prophase can still condense its chromosomes (1) and arrange them in the middle (2), because those do not need chromatids to separate. It cannot complete anaphase (3) or telophase to form two cells (4), because those depend on successful separation. So only 1 and 2 can occur.

options.A: Correct. Prophase (1) and metaphase (2) occur before sister chromatid separation, so they are not blocked by a spindle poison.
options.B: Not correct. While 2 can occur, 3 is anaphase which requires chromatids to separate and move apart, exactly what the drug prevents.
options.C: Not complete. Cell 2 alone misses cell 1, but prophase condensation (1) does not need the spindle to pull chromatids apart, so it can also occur.
options.D: Not correct. Both 3 (anaphase) and 4 (telophase) depend on successful separation of chromatids, so both are blocked by this drug.
